      </code>
    </td>
  </tr>
</tbody>
</table>

```text
deleteById               destructive, idempotent  — "delete"
createPersonIfNotExist   idempotent               — the suffix rule is reached before "create"
peopleCount              read-only                — "count", though it does not lead the name
getOrCreatePerson        all three false          — "create" is reached before "get"
notifyPeople             all three false          — no rule matches
```

The adds-or-acts row exists only to be reached before the reads row. `getOrCreatePerson` both reads and creates, and matching it there is what stops `readOnlyHint = true` from being served for a call that creates a person. All three `false` is not "unknown" — it is the honest answer, and it tells a host the tool may modify something and is not safe to run unattended.

Every hint is always written to the wire, which matters most for `openWorldHint`: [MCP defaults it to `true`](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/server/tools), so a tool that omits it is read as one that may call out to any external system, and hosts weigh that when deciding whether a call needs approval. A Kinotic function works against the platform's own data, so the served default is `false`; a function that does reach a third-party system says so:

```java
@McpTool(openWorldHint = true)
Future<Project> retryRepoInitialization(String projectId);
```

Nothing in a function's name says whether it calls out, so `openWorldHint` is never inferred — only a declaration sets it.

A function with a streaming return type (`Flux`, `Publisher`) cannot be a tool — registration fails with an error naming the function, and a server registering the service as it starts does not start. Single-value async returns (`Future`, `CompletableFuture`, `Mono`) are fine.

## Tool naming

The tool name is the XXHash128 of the service's qualified name plus the function, written in base 36:

```text
app.acme-org.orders-app~com.acme.OrderService/findById
  → 5nwldv2gqljeygvmd1ywjl2z7
```

Because a qualified name is unique system wide, so is its hash — every caller scope, including system participants who see every zone, gets an unambiguous listing. Names are never parsed back apart: resolution is a caller-scoped directory query, and authorization reads the zone from the tool's stored CRI.

A name is opaque, so `title` and `description` are what an LLM has to work with, and both are always served — the description leading with the title, for hosts that show the model nothing else. Base 36 also bounds a name at 25 characters however long the service's package is, well inside the 128-character MCP limit.

`KinoticUtil.mcpToolName(qualifiedName, functionName)` mints the name, so anything that needs to name a tool it did not read from a listing computes the same value the directory stored:

```java
KinoticUtil.mcpToolName("management-api~org.kinotic.management.api.services.ProjectService", "findByRepoFullName")
```

Hashing is what keeps a name safe to pass through an LLM host. MCP permits characters in a tool name that hosts do not — a dot most commonly — and a host rewrites each one, then holds two names for the same tool: the one the server advertises and the one it calls. Any layer that compares the wrong pair breaks, and the failure is invisible from the server. A permission granted against the advertised name and checked against the callable one leaves a tool that prompts for approval, is approved, and reports that it still needs approval. Base 36 emits only `[0-9a-z]`, so a host has nothing to rewrite.

## The endpoint

The org and system servers serve MCP; the app server does not. A server that runs management-api's services without an API gateway, such as a UI's backend built on Kinotic, sets `kinotic.managementApi.disableMcpServer: true` to leave the MCP server out. `POST /mcp` speaks the stateless streamable-HTTP subset of MCP: JSON-RPC 2.0 with `initialize`, `notifications/initialized`, `ping`, `tools/list`, and `tools/call`. There are no sessions — every request authenticates independently from its headers, exactly like a STOMP `CONNECT`. Other verbs return 405, and JSON-RPC batches are rejected.

## Authorization

Two ways in, both landing on the same participant model:

**OAuth 2.1 (MCP authorization spec)** — what Claude connectors, Claude Code plugins, and other MCP hosts use. An unauthenticated request gets `401` with `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata="…/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp"`, from which a host discovers the authorization server (RFC 9728 + RFC 8414, both served under the server's issuer: on the management server `kinotic.managementServer.issuerBaseUrl`, which falls back to `kinotic.managementApi.apiBaseUrl`; on the system server `kinotic.systemServer.apiBaseUrl`; on the app server the application's own API host), identifies itself with a [Client ID Metadata Document](https://kinotic.ai/platform/system-security#client-identity-is-a-domain-not-a-string) URL, and runs the PKCE S256 authorization-code flow: `GET /api/auth/oauth/authorize` sends the browser to the `/oauth/consent` page of the server's UI, where the signed-in user approves (the page sends `POST /api/auth/oauth/approve` with the login its own session holds), and `POST /api/auth/oauth/token` (form-encoded) exchanges the single-use code for a one-hour access token plus a rotating 90-day refresh token (`offline_access` is advertised, so hosts refresh without re-consent; refresh-token reuse revokes the whole token family).

The issued token's `sub` is a delegate identity created when the user approves the consent — the host acts on that user's behalf, at the user's exact scope, as a `SystemParticipant`, `OrganizationParticipant`, or `ApplicationParticipant` carrying `onBehalfOf` metadata, and sees the same visibility matrix as every other caller. Approving the same host again reuses the delegate, and disabling it revokes the host's access on its next request from the **Connected apps** page of whichever client the owner signs in to — the portal for an organization account, the system console for a system user's. Which account is signing the approval therefore decides the host's reach, so the consent page names it: a `SystemParticipant` delegate is filtered by no zone and sees every organization's tools, which the page warns about before the operator approves. A Claude Code plugin needs nothing beyond the server URL:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "kinotic-os": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://api.kinotic.ai/mcp"
    }
  }
}
```

There is no registration endpoint. Dynamic Client Registration (RFC 7591) is not supported: a `client_id` is the HTTPS URL of the client's own metadata document, which the gateway fetches and validates per authorization request. That URL must appear in `kinotic.domain.oauth.allowedClientIds`, which ships with the document URLs of [Claude Code and the Claude connectors](https://kinotic.ai/platform/system-security#client-identity-is-a-domain-not-a-string), plus ChatGPT, Codex, Grok, and Grok Build on the management server; a host whose URL is absent gets `400 {"error":"invalid_request"}` from `/api/auth/oauth/authorize`.

The management server's `kinotic.managementServer.issuerBaseUrl` is separate from its API base URL, `kinotic.managementApi.apiBaseUrl`, because the two are reached by different parties. A browser follows the OIDC callbacks built from the API base URL; an MCP host's backend calls the token endpoint built from `issuerBaseUrl`, having never been near the browser. They are the same URL in any deployment the internet reaches directly, and differ where the gateway is public only through a tunnel or a separate ingress — a development gateway on `localhost` whose OAuth surface is tunnelled, for instance, keeps its OIDC callbacks (and its IdP app registrations) on `localhost` while publishing a reachable token endpoint.

**Static headers** — for agent frameworks and scripts that can attach headers: `clientId`/`clientSecret` (plus `organizationId` to select an organization's user on the management server; the system server's users take none), or `Authorization: Bearer <kinotic-jwt>`. A bearer token takes its scope from the token's own claims, which are not cross-checked against any scope headers sent alongside it. Each server admits only its own kind of caller, so an organization's credentials authenticate at the management server's `/mcp` and a system user's at the system server's.

`tools/list` is paginated per the [MCP pagination spec](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/server/utilities/pagination): a response carrying `nextCursor` has more results, fetched by repeating the request with that opaque `cursor`; an invalid cursor is rejected with `-32602`. It returns the tools the authenticated participant may call through this server, mirroring the zone send rules the gateway enforces at call time: a system participant sees every zone, and an organization participant sees `management-api`- and `app-api`-zone tools and those of its own applications, under `app.<org>`, each zone with its sub-zones. Application participants reach no MCP endpoint: the org and system servers refuse them, and the app server serves none. Each server lists only the zones it reaches: the system server's MCP endpoint shows `system-api`- and `management-api`-zone tools even to a system participant. Offline services' tools are not listed.

`tools/call` dispatches through the same RPC path as every other service invocation, with the caller's participant as the sender. Resolution and dispatch are independently authorized — see [Defense in Depth](https://kinotic.ai/platform/defense-in-depth). The `arguments` object is delivered to the service bound by parameter name, so the names in the tool's input schema are exactly the names the service binds. A call to an offline service or an invocation error returns an MCP tool error (`isError: true`) with the message as text content.


# Observability

> Monitoring, tracing, and logging across your Kinotic applications.

## Overview

Kinotic provides deep observability across your applications, aggregated at multiple levels: System, Organization, and Application.

## Metrics

Real-time monitoring of CPU, memory, and data throughput for all running services. Metrics are collected automatically for every deployed application and available through the Kinotic dashboard.

## Traces and Spans

Drill from high-level overviews into detailed execution logs. Distributed tracing follows requests across service boundaries, so you can pinpoint performance bottlenecks and errors in complex service interactions. A workload running in a micro VM ships its traces and metrics through the node that runs it — see [Workload Traces and Metrics](#workload-traces-and-metrics) — and the portal shows them on an application's **Observability** page, and across the organization at **Observability** in the organization sidebar.

## LLM Observability

Trace user interactions with LLMs and track token utilization for cost analysis. LLM request and response data is indexed via Grafana Loki, giving you full-text search across all LLM interactions with filtering by user, application, model, and time range.

## Audit Logs

Track platform activity including:

- **Login history** — Who connected, when, and from where
- **Configuration changes** — OIDC provider updates, LLM configuration changes, and application settings modifications
- **Activity counts** — Aggregate usage metrics per user, application, and organization

## Application Logs

View microservice logs directly from the dashboard with the ability to temporarily adjust logging levels for debugging. Increase verbosity on a running service to investigate an issue, then restore normal levels when done — no redeployment required.

The same dialog edits a node's [trace log filters](https://kinotic.ai/platform/configuration#trace-logging), so turning a logger up to TRACE does not have to mean drowning in whatever service talks most. Both changes last until the node restarts.

The servers' own logs are in Loki's `kinotic-system` tenant, and every stream of them carries two labels: `service_name`, the server (`kinotic-server-management`, `kinotic-server-system` or `kinotic-server-app`), and `service_instance_id`, the node. Each node reads both from its `OTEL_SERVICE_NAME` and the `service.instance.id` in its `OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES`, and every deployment sets them to match how its logs are shipped:

<table>
<thead>
  <tr>
    <th>
      Deployment
    </th>
    
    <th>
      How the logs reach Loki
    </th>
    
    <th>
      <code>
        service.instance.id
      </code>
    </th>
  </tr>
</thead>

<tbody>
  <tr>
    <td>
      Development server
    </td>
    
    <td>
      The OpenTelemetry agent, which labels them from those same settings
    </td>
    
    <td>
      The server's name and the container's vmid, <code>
        kinotic-server-app-123
      </code>
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      Compose
    </td>
    
    <td>
      The OpenTelemetry agent, as above
    </td>
    
    <td>
      The container's name
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      Kubernetes
    </td>

      Alloy, from each pod's output, labelling the server pods' streams from their <code>
        app
      </code>
      
       label and pod name
    </td>
    
    <td>
      The pod's name
    </td>
  </tr>
</tbody>
</table>

The system console's Cluster page lists each server node with the server it runs (`management`, `system` or `app`) and its Kinotic version, and its **Logs** button shows that node's logs alone. A node with no `service.instance.id` shows every node of its server interleaved, and one with no `OTEL_SERVICE_NAME` shows no button. `LogService.tailServer` and `LogService.serverHistory` read them, for a system participant alone.

The log view, here and for a workload's logs, loads the selected time range and follows new lines only once its **Follow** button is pressed. It shows an entry that spans several lines as one row per line under the entry's timestamp, and renders the ANSI color and style escapes a line carries as a terminal would. An entry shipped with an OpenTelemetry `severity_text` shows that level beside its timestamp, colored as Spring Boot's console colors it, an entry shipped with a `scope_name` (the OpenTelemetry agent sets it to the logger's name) shows that logger before its message, abbreviated as Spring Boot's console abbreviates it, and an entry shipped with an `exception_stacktrace` (the OpenTelemetry agent keeps a logged exception there rather than in the message) shows the stack trace under its message.

## Workload Logs

Logs from micro VM workloads (builds, deploys, and application containers) are shipped to Grafana Loki and can be tailed live or queried historically, per workload.

The workload runner starts the processes it runs (the sync's install, entity sync and UI builds, and an application's microservice) with `FORCE_COLOR=1`, unless the workload sets its own `FORCE_COLOR`, so tools that honor it, such as bun, chalk and picocolors, keep the ANSI colors they would print to a terminal, and the log view renders them.

### Log shipping architecture

Every node runs a managed [Grafana Alloy](https://grafana.com/docs/alloy/latest/) process whose pipeline is regenerated as workloads come and go; Alloy tails each running workload's log files and pushes them to Loki, and receives the traces and metrics of the workloads that elect telemetry and pushes them to Tempo and Mimir (see [Workload Traces and Metrics](#workload-traces-and-metrics)). What a workload has to do for its logs to be shipped depends on the node's [VM provider](https://kinotic.ai/platform/configuration#vm-provider):

<table>
<thead>
  <tr>
    <th>
      Provider
    </th>
    
    <th>
      What is shipped
    </th>
    
    <th>
      What the workload must do
    </th>
  </tr>
</thead>

<tbody>
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        CLOUD_HYPERVISOR
      </code>
    </td>
    
    <td>
      The workload's stdout and stderr, captured by the container runtime
    </td>
    
    <td>
      Nothing — write to stdout and stderr
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        BOXLITE
      </code>
    </td>
    
    <td>
      Any <code>
        *.log
      </code>
      
       file under <code>
        /var/log/kinotic
      </code>
      
      , a per-workload host directory mounted into the VM
    </td>
    
    <td>
      Write log files into that directory itself. The node names it as <code>
        KINOTIC_LOG_DIR
      </code>
      
       in the guest environment, with the <code>
        logPolicy
      </code>
      
       as <code>
        KINOTIC_LOG_MAX_SIZE_MB
      </code>
      
       and <code>
        KINOTIC_LOG_MAX_FILES
      </code>
      
      ; the workload-runner image honours this, writing a size-rotated <code>
        workload.log
      </code>
      
       there
    </td>
  </tr>
</tbody>
</table>

`CLOUD_HYPERVISOR` nodes label each stream `stdout` or `stderr`. Both providers bound what a workload's logs occupy on the node through `logPolicy` — `maxSizeMb` is the size at which the current file rotates, and `maxFiles` how many rotated files are kept beside it — the container runtime enforcing it on `CLOUD_HYPERVISOR`, and the image itself on `BOXLITE`.

Workload VMs run detached from the vm-manager process by default (`Workload.detached`), and the vm-manager persists each workload's state on the node. If the vm-manager restarts (a crash, a systemd restart), it reattaches to the detached VMs that are still running and regenerates the Alloy pipeline, so their logs keep shipping. A non-detached workload runs in the foreground — the call that starts it resolves only once its run has ended, with the exit code — and ends with the vm-manager process.

On a deployment's job run page the **Sync project source** step expands into the sync workload's log, the way a CI step does: open while the step runs, where its **Follow** button follows new lines as they arrive, and readable afterwards from the run's history. The node's removal of an ended run waits for the shipper to read the workload's log files to the end first, so a run over in seconds still ships every line it wrote, and a workload's logs outlive its VM: they are read by the organization and workload id, so the sync and publish workloads, which the node removes as their runs end, stay readable from the run's history until the workload's record is deleted — from the console, or by the retention sweep once the run is older than `kinotic.systemApi.workload.retentionDays` — which deletes its log streams with it (see [Workload retention](https://kinotic.ai/platform/configuration#workload-retention)).

A run that has ended — stopped, exited, or failed — is removed from the node once the server holds its outcome: the node ships what the VM wrote, then removes the VM, its disk and its log files. The workload's record and its logs remain until the record is deleted, so a microservice restart from the console runs a fresh VM with a new `vm_id`.

Every log stream carries these labels:

<table>
<thead>
  <tr>
    <th>
      Label
    </th>
    
    <th>
      Value
    </th>
  </tr>
</thead>

<tbody>
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        workload_id
      </code>
    </td>
    
    <td>
      The workload's id
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        vm_id
      </code>
    </td>
    
    <td>
      The provider's id for the micro VM
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        stream
      </code>
    </td>
    
    <td>
      <code>
        stdout
      </code>
      
       or <code>
        stderr
      </code>
      
      , on <code>
        CLOUD_HYPERVISOR
      </code>
      
       nodes
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        node_id
      </code>
    </td>
    
    <td>
      The vm-manager node the workload runs on
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        application_id
      </code>
    </td>
    
    <td>
      The workload's application, when it has one
    </td>
  </tr>
</tbody>
</table>

Loki runs multi-tenant. A workload's logs are stored in its organization's tenant (`X-Scope-OrgID` = the organization id), so one organization's queries can never see another's streams. System workloads with no organization ship to the reserved `kinotic-system` tenant — organization ids beginning with `kinotic` are reserved for the system. System users can query across tenants with pipe-separated ids (for example `acme|kinotic-system`).

### Reading workload logs

The `LogService` (`@kinotic-ai/management-api`) streams (`tail`) and queries (`history`) the logs of workloads the caller may view: an organization participant sees its own organization's workloads, a system participant sees any. Its `tailServer` and `serverHistory` read a Kinotic server's logs the same way (see [Application Logs](#application-logs)). A history covers its range up to but excluding its `end`, and a tail starts at the moment it is given, including it: it first sends the entries since then and then each new one, so a tail started at a history's `end` reads on from it with no entry repeated or missed, which is how the console's log view follows. Every method returns raw Loki response bytes for the caller to parse.

## Workload Traces and Metrics

A workload that sets `telemetry` to `true` is given an OTLP endpoint of its own on the node it runs on, and the traces and metrics it exports there are shipped to Tempo and Mimir under its organization's tenant, carrying the same identity as its log streams. Telemetry is elected per workload: the node ships nothing for a workload that leaves it off, whatever the workload's runtime exports. The runtime workload of every [deployed project](https://kinotic.ai/platform/configuration#project-deployment) elects it, under the project's name as its service name.

### What the node does

When the workload's VM is created the node issues it an endpoint — a host port its Alloy listens on for that workload alone, and a bearer token only that guest is given — and names it in the guest environment through the standard OpenTelemetry variables, which every OpenTelemetry SDK reads:

<table>
<thead>
  <tr>
    <th>
      Variable
    </th>
    
    <th>
      Value
    </th>
  </tr>
</thead>

<tbody>
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT
      </code>
    </td>
    
    <td>
      <code>
        http://<the node, as the guest reaches it>:<port>
      </code>
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL
      </code>
    </td>

        http/protobuf
      </code>
    </td>
  </tr>

  </tr>

      </code>
    </td>

      The workload's name, unless the workload's own <code>
        environment
      </code>
      
       sets it
    </td>
  </tr>
</tbody>
</table>

The exporter variables are laid over the workload's own `environment` and `secrets`, so a workload cannot point its exporter elsewhere by setting them itself; the service name is the one variable the workload may set, since it is how its spans and metrics are grouped. The endpoint holds for the workload's life, restarts included, and is released when the workload is destroyed. Each receiver accepts only its own token, so a guest cannot push into another workload's stream. A workload electing telemetry on a node that ships neither signal runs without an endpoint.

### What the workload must do

Export over OTLP from that environment. An OpenTelemetry SDK configured from the environment — the Java agent, or the Node SDK with its default configuration — does so without any code of its own. The Kinotic runtimes instrument every service invocation through the OpenTelemetry API, so a Kinotic application whose process runs such an SDK ships a span per call, continuing the trace of the caller that invoked it. A runtime that ignores the variables ships nothing.

A deployed project needs nothing of its own: the `workload-runner` image preloads the Node SDK into the microservice process, started only when the endpoint variable is present and flushing its pending spans when the process is stopped. The SDK registers against the global OpenTelemetry API, which the project's own `@opentelemetry/api` — the one `@kinotic-ai/core` records through — resolves as long as it is the same major version and no newer than the image's. A project that starts an SDK of its own finds the API already registered, so that SDK exports nothing: leave the bootstrap to the image.

A workload with `network.mode` `DISABLED` has no way to reach the endpoint, so a node refuses one that also elects telemetry rather than starting it silent.

### How a guest reaches its endpoint

<table>
<thead>
  <tr>
    <th>
      Provider
    </th>
    
    <th>

    </th>
    
    <th>

    </th>
  </tr>
</thead>

<tbody>
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        CLOUD_HYPERVISOR
      </code>
    </td>
    
    <td>
      The docker bridge gateway (<code>
        172.17.0.1
      </code>
      
       unless the daemon is configured otherwise)
    </td>
    
    <td>
      Binds the receiver to that address alone and opens the workload's port to the workload's address in the host firewall, above the floor that shields the node's own services from every guest
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>

      </code>

    </td>

    </td>
  </tr>
</tbody>
</table>

The port is opened by the same per-workload rules as the workload's [egress](https://kinotic.ai/platform/configuration#workload-egress), so a `CLOUD_HYPERVISOR` node that does not deny egress by default refuses a workload electing telemetry, as it refuses one declaring `allowedHosts`.

### Identity and tenant

Every span and every metric arrives with these resource attributes, matching the labels on the workload's log streams:

<table>
<thead>
  <tr>
    <th>
      Attribute
    </th>
    
    <th>
      Value
    </th>
  </tr>
</thead>

<tbody>
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        workload_id
      </code>
    </td>
    
    <td>
      The workload's id
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        vm_id
      </code>
    </td>
    
    <td>
      The provider's id for the micro VM
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        node_id
      </code>
    </td>
    
    <td>
      The vm-manager node the workload runs on
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        application_id
      </code>
    </td>
    
    <td>
      The workload's application, when it has one
    </td>
  </tr>
</tbody>
</table>

Traces and metrics are pushed with `X-Scope-OrgID` set to the organization id, or `kinotic-system` for system workloads with no organization — the same tenant the logs go to. Tempo and Mimir run multi-tenant (`multitenancy_enabled: true`, as the docker-compose stack and the Kubernetes deployment set them), so each organization's telemetry is kept apart the way Loki keeps its logs, and Tempo's metrics-generator writes the span metrics it derives — `traces_spanmetrics_calls_total`, `traces_spanmetrics_latency_bucket` — into the same tenant, carrying `application_id` and `workload_id` beside `service` so one application's RED metrics can be selected within its organization.

The platform servers name the backend each of their HTTP client spans called as its `peer.service` — `elasticsearch`, `loki`, `tempo`, or `mimir` — and the span metrics carry it as `peer_service`, so a query over the system tenant can select those calls or leave them out: `sum by (span_name) (rate(traces_spanmetrics_calls_total{peer_service!="elasticsearch"}[5m]))` charts the servers' work without the bare `GET` / `POST` spans of their Elasticsearch calls.

### Reading workload traces and metrics

The `TelemetryService` (`@kinotic-ai/management-api`, `Kinotic.telemetry`) searches traces (`searchTraces`, a TraceQL query over a time range), fetches one trace with all its spans (`findTrace`), and evaluates PromQL (`queryMetrics`, a range query at a step). Each call names an organization: an organization participant may name only its own, and a system participant any, or none for the system's own telemetry. The tenant is the boundary; what a query selects within it is the caller's to decide. All three return the raw Tempo and Prometheus response bytes for the caller to parse.

The portal shows them on an application's **Observability** page: a trace search — by service, span name, errors, and duration — opening each trace on its own page as a waterfall of its spans with their attributes, and the requests, errors, and latency of the calls the application's services handle (their server spans, so the calls a service makes, such as to Elasticsearch, stay out of its numbers) beside a free PromQL query, the errors chart leading to the traces with a failed span. The organization's **Observability** page has the same view across all of its applications or one of them, and so does the system console at **Organizations → (organization) → Observability**, with each application's view under **Applications → (application) → Observability**. The console's own **Observability** page, under System, reads the system tenant: the traces and metrics of the servers, the gateway, and the worker nodes themselves.

    </td>
    
    <td>
      Tempo HTTP API the server queries (default <code>
        http://localhost:3200
      </code>
      
      )
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        kinotic.managementApi.mimirUrl
      </code>
      
       / <code>
        KINOTIC_MANAGEMENTAPI_MIMIRURL
      </code>
      
       (server)
    </td>
    
    <td>
      Mimir HTTP API the server queries, whose Prometheus API is under <code>
        /prometheus
      </code>
      
       (default <code>
        http://localhost:9009
      </code>
      
      )
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        KINOTIC_TEMPO_URL
      </code>
      
       (vm-manager)
    </td>
    
    <td>
      Base URL of the OTLP/HTTP endpoint the node's Alloy pushes traces to — Tempo's own (<code>
        http://tempo:4318
      </code>
      
      ), or a collector in front of it; unset disables trace shipping
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        KINOTIC_MIMIR_URL
      </code>
      
       (vm-manager)
    </td>
    
    <td>
      Base URL of the OTLP/HTTP endpoint the node's Alloy pushes metrics to — Mimir's own (<code>
        http://mimir:9009/otlp
      </code>
      
      ), or a collector in front of it; unset disables metric shipping
    </td>
  </tr>
</tbody>
</table>

The vm-manager resolves the Alloy binary from the `PATH`, downloading its pinned release when none is found. Both the download and Alloy's launch happen while the node starts up, before it registers and accepts workloads, so no workload operation waits on them. One Alloy process ships logs, traces, and metrics; a node configured for some of them runs it for those alone.


# Organization Management

> How organizations are created, how their users authenticate, and how OIDC providers are wired up.

## Overview

A Kinotic deployment hosts many customer organizations. Each org has its own users, applications, and (optionally) its own enterprise SSO configuration. This page describes how an org is created, who can log in to it, and how the OIDC plumbing is shared across orgs without leaking access between them.

System users sign in to the system server, separately from everything described here; see [System Authentication](#system-authentication).

## Mental Model

Eight persistent entities carry the auth state, and one short-lived entity bridges each signup. The [Sign-In Design](https://kinotic.ai/platform/reference/sign-in-design) reference draws them and the flows between them.

A configuration is offered at the one scope its kind names. When the same Okta tenant serves both the org's own login and one of its applications', the org copies the configuration into the application's scope with `OwnedOidcConfigurationService.copy`; the copy is registered with the provider under its own callback URL and keeps its own copy of the client secret. An application offers the system's Google and Microsoft registrations by naming their provider kinds in its `socialProviders`.

### Two distinct OIDC roles

The roles are separate *subtypes* of `OidcConfiguration`, stored in one index under a `type` discriminator the way the kinds of `ParticipantIdentity` are, rather than one type with a flag, because the difference between them is ownership. Every lookup filters on the discriminator and every write is held to its kind's owner, so an org admin configuring SSO can never make it appear as a global button or name a system secret, and a seeded system registration can never affect an org's SSO settings.

## Org Creation

There are two entry points, both producing an `Organization` and an admin `ParticipantIdentity` scoped to it. The SPA's `/signup` page currently offers **GitHub only** (a hardcoded button — every Kinotic project is backed by a GitHub repository, so the founding user signs up with GitHub and installs the GitHub App right after). The email/password signup entry point remains fully mounted on the backend; its previous UI (`Signup.vue`) is kept in the tree unrouted until other methods return. Login is not restricted: invitees must be able to sign back in however they joined, so an organization's login page keeps every provider the organization offers plus a password form.

### Email/password signup (backend flow — not currently reachable from the SPA)

```text
1. User loads /signup, enters email + displayName
2. POST /api/auth/org/signup
3. SignUpService.initiateLocalSignUp:
   - rejects if a sign-up is already pending for this email, or if an organization user
     already exists for this email: a person founds one organization at most, and joins
     others by invitation. When that organization user is a member an administrator added
     that nobody signs in as yet, the refusal (PendingMemberException) says to accept the
     invitation or sign in on that organization's sign-in page
   - creates a PendingSignUp with a 24h verification token
   - EmailService sends the verification link (logs it instead when email is disabled), which
     opens the portal
4. User clicks /signup/verify?token=<verificationToken> in their inbox
5. /signup/verify form (VerifyEmail.vue) prompts for orgName + password + confirm
6. POST /api/auth/org/signup/complete  { token, orgName, orgDescription?, password }
7. SignUpService.completeLocalSignUp:
   - validates token, rejects if expired
   - creates Organization (auto-derived id from name)
   - creates the founder's organization user (OrganizationParticipantIdentity,
     enabled=true) with an IdentityCredential (bcrypt hash, separate index keyed by the
     organization user's id)
   - creates the founder's OrganizationMembership of the organization
   - links Organization.createdBy = the organization user's id
   - deletes the PendingSignUp
8. The gateway establishes the browser session (204 + Set-Cookie); the frontend then calls
   userState.login() to open the realtime connection, authenticated by that session cookie.
```

Email verification is the security gate — no `Organization`, organization user or membership exists until the link is clicked. With `KINOTIC_EMAIL_ENABLED=false` (the local default) the verification URL is logged to the management server's console instead of sent; copy it into the browser to finish the flow.

### Social-IdP signup

```text
1. User loads /signup, clicks "Sign up with GitHub" (the page's only button today)
2. POST /api/auth/org/signup/social/start/github
3. OrganizationSignupHandler.handleSocialStart:
   - picks the OrgSignupOidcConfiguration whose provider key matches
     (oidcConfigurationService.findEnabledOrgSignupByProvider)
   - generates state/nonce/PKCE, stashes them on the session cookie
   - 302 to <authority>/authorize?...
4. User authenticates at the IdP
5. IdP returns to GET /api/auth/org/login/social/callback/<configId>, the one callback the
   registration is registered with; the flow's purpose, recorded at its start, routes it
6. OrganizationOidcCallbackHandler → OrganizationSignupHandler.complete:
   - validates state/nonce/PKCE, exchanges code for id_token + access_token
   - rejects if email_verified=false in the id_token
   - SignUpService.createOidcPending rejects with user_exists if an organization user is
     already bound to (configId, sub) or holds the verified email: a person founds one
     organization at most, and joins others by invitation. It rejects with user_pending when
     that organization user is a member an administrator added that nobody signs in as yet,
     who gets in through their invitation or the organization's own provider. SignUpService
     checks again at completion, so two sign-ups of one identity
     in flight at once cannot both found an organization, and the organization is never
     created for an organization user that cannot be
   - creates a PendingSignUp with the verified subject, configId, email, displayName
   - 302 to /register?token=<verificationToken> on the UI the sign-up started from, when
     kinotic.domain.cors.allowedOriginPattern names its origin other than through *, and on the portal otherwise
7. /register prompts for orgName (CompleteOrg.vue)
8. POST /api/auth/org/signup/social/complete  { token, orgName, orgDescription? }
9. SignUpService.completeOidcWithNewOrg:
   - validates the pending token
   - creates Organization
   - creates the founder's organization user (enabled=true) with an OidcBinding of
     (configId, sub) to it
   - creates the founder's OrganizationMembership of the organization
   - links Organization.createdBy
   - deletes the PendingSignUp
10. The gateway establishes the browser session (204 + Set-Cookie). CompleteOrg.vue then
    calls userState.login() to open the realtime connection, authenticated by that session
    cookie. No token travels in the URL.
11. CompleteOrg.vue shows a "Connect GitHub" step explaining that the next GitHub
    round-trip authorizes repository access (distinct from the sign-in, which only
    proved identity). Clicking "Continue to GitHub" calls
    githubAppInstallations.startInstall("/") and redirects the whole tab to
    the returned GitHub install URL. The App requests user authorization (OAuth) during
    installation, so GitHub returns to the management server's /api/github/install/callback
    — the App's first registered callback URL — with code, installation_id, and the state
    minted by startInstall, and that route forwards them to the portal's
    /github/install/callback. The callback runs completeInstall, which consumes the state, exchanges
    the code with the github-platform credential for the authorizing user's access
    token, and binds the installation only when GitHub's /user/installations reports
    that user can access it (see [Defense in Depth](/platform/defense-in-depth)). It
    then lands on / — project creation requires the install, so the new org arrives
    ready. If the install can't start, the page falls back to / directly. The portal's /
    opens the Quickstart until the organization has its first project, and Applications
    after that.
```

Another UI signed in through the management server, such as one built on Kinotic, links GitHub
without the portal: it calls `startInstall` with the absolute URL of one of its own pages as
`returnTo`, which must be on an origin `kinotic.domain.cors.allowedOriginPattern` names (a pattern of
`*` names none);
`startInstall` refuses any other URL, and a network-path reference (a `returnTo` starting with `//`
or `/\`). After the install, `/api/github/install/callback` forwards GitHub's `installation_id`,
`state` and `code` to that page as query parameters, and the page calls `completeInstall` itself.

The `PendingSignUp` is consumed once. The `?token=` in the redirect to `/register` is the short-lived `PendingSignUp` verification token. It is not a login, which the session cookie set when the org-naming POST succeeds establishes, but whoever holds it can found the organization as the verified identity, so it is handed only to a UI the CORS pattern trusts.

GitHub follows the same flow with one difference in step 6: GitHub is OAuth 2.0 only and issues no id_token, so its configuration row sets the endpoints explicitly instead of relying on discovery — `authorizationUri`/`tokenUri` drive the code flow, `userInfoUri` supplies `sub` and the display name, and `userEmailsUri` supplies the email plus its `verified` flag (primary address preferred). Any curated row that sets these fields takes this path; nothing about it is GitHub-specific in code, and only a curated row can set them. Issuer, audience, and nonce validation don't apply (there is no token to carry them); the state match and the direct TLS code exchange are the security boundary.

## Members

An organization's administrators add its members on the Members page, one action for every case: **Add member**, with the person's email, an optional display name and a switch, on by default, that sends them an invitation email (`MemberService.addMember(email, displayName, sendInvitation)`, `Kinotic.members.addMember`).

- **An address with no organization user yet** gets one, with no sign-in method, and its membership at once, so the person appears among the members as *Pending*. With the switch on, the invitation they receive claims the organization user: they set a password, or sign in through one of the organization's providers under the same address. With the switch off, nothing is sent and the person signs in through one of the organization's own providers (`OrganizationOidcConfiguration`), whose first sign-in under the invited address claims the organization user — so the switch can only be off when the organization has one, and the server refuses the request otherwise, revealing nothing about the address.
- **An address that already has an organization user** is emailed an invitation whatever the switch says, since joining someone's organization user to an organization needs their acceptance; they appear once they accept, and the administrator is told an invitation was sent. Accepting with that organization user's password, or through one of the organization's providers whose verified email is the invited one, joins it. A system user or an application's user with the same address is a different identity, which neither the invitation nor the member list sees: the address joins as a new organization user with a password of its own.
- **Pending members** are listed with the invitations alike, each with *Send invitation* (`MemberService.sendInvitation(email)`, which sends the one they have again or a new one for a member added without) and *Remove*. Removing a pending member deletes the organization user nobody signed in as and the invitation it never accepted; removing a member who has signed in leaves their organization user and other organizations as they are.
- **An application's users** are still invited (`MemberService.inviteMember(email, displayName, applicationId)`), since their rows belong to the application and are created when the invitation is accepted.

### Email templates

The portal's invitations and verification links open the portal and use Kinotic's own emails. A server
that embeds Kinotic's modules to serve a UI of its own sends them in that UI's name instead, by passing an
`EmailTemplate` in process: management-api's `MemberInvitationService.addMember`, `sendInvitation` and
`inviteMember` (the calls `MemberService` makes, run as the organization user bound to the call) and
kinotic-domain's `SignUpService.initiateLocalSignUp`. `EmailTemplate` is not part of any published service, so no
gateway connection can choose one.

A template's `uiBaseUrl` is the UI whose `/invite/accept?token=` or `/signup/verify?token=` page its link
opens, with no trailing slash, and its `subject`, `htmlBody` and `textBody` are Handlebars sources rendered
with the email's variables. A call that would send an email with a template whose `uiBaseUrl` is not an absolute
http or https URL naming a host, without user info, a query, fragment or trailing slash, or whose source is missing
or does not compile and render, fails with
`IllegalArgumentException` before it saves anything. Write a URL variable in the HTML with triple braces, such as `{{{acceptUrl}}}`, so it is not
HTML-escaped.

<table>
<thead>
  <tr>
    <th>
      Email
    </th>
    
    <th>
      Variables
    </th>
  </tr>
</thead>

<tbody>
  <tr>
    <td>
      An invitation into an organization or one of its applications
    </td>
    
    <td>
      <code>
        inviterName
      </code>
      
      , <code>
        organizationName
      </code>
      
      , <code>
        applicationName
      </code>
      
       (absent for an organization invitation), <code>
        acceptUrl
      </code>
      
      , <code>
        expiresInDays
      </code>
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      A sign-up with email and password
    </td>
    
    <td>
      <code>
        displayName
      </code>
      
      , <code>
        verificationUrl
      </code>
    </td>
  </tr>
</tbody>
</table>

That UI's invitation page calls the `/api/auth/invite/*` routes below. An acceptance through a provider
returns to the page that started it, and a failed one to that page's `/invite/accept?error=`, when
that page is the portal or `kinotic.domain.cors.allowedOriginPattern` names it, and to the portal otherwise. An
application invitation whose application has its own invitation template is sent with that template's
content, and its link still opens the passed template's UI.

The Members page lists the organization's members as `OrganizationMember` rows (`MemberService.findMembers` / `searchMembers`): each joins an organization user with its membership, so `enabled` is the membership's standing, `joined` its creation, and `pending` marks a member who has not signed in yet. An application's Users page lists the application's users themselves, `ApplicationParticipantIdentity` rows (`MemberService.findApplicationUsers` / `searchApplicationUsers`), whose standing is the user's own.

An organization's own provider therefore signs in only the members its administrators added: a person the provider verifies whose address no pending member holds gets `no_user`, and `createUserOnSignIn` is refused on an `OrganizationOidcConfiguration`. Nothing an organization's provider asserts can reach an organization user the organization did not create, and an organization user someone already signs in as joins only by its holder's acceptance.

## User Login

A login is addressed to an organization. An organization user may be a member of any number of organizations, each an `OrganizationMembership` of its own, so nothing about the person alone says where they are signing in; the organization's id, the slug of its hostnames (see [Applications and Projects](https://kinotic.ai/apps/application-structure/applications-and-projects#applications)), is what every login route and page is addressed by. The portal has two login pages:

- `/login`, the landing page, for someone whose organization is not yet known: the system's social buttons, which sign in without naming an organization when the identity belongs to exactly one and otherwise offer the ones it belongs to; an organization field that leads to that organization's page; and a "Don't know your organization?" link that emails the person the organizations their address belongs to.
- `/login/<organizationId>`, the organization's page (`OrganizationLoginPage.vue`), which offers exactly what that organization's login supports: one button per configuration `GET /api/auth/org/login/<organizationId>/providers` lists — the system's org sign-up registrations (GitHub) followed by the organization's own `OrganizationOidcConfiguration`s — and an email + password form. The organization's own host, `<organizationId>.<sitesDomain>`, redirects here.

The browser remembers, in `localStorage`, the organization it last signed in to, whichever method signed it in: password, GitHub, an organization's own provider, sign-up, an accepted invitation or a switch of organizations. A returning browser that opens `/login` is sent on to that organization's page, keeping the query and so the `referer`. The landing page stays put when nothing is remembered, and when its query carries `?error=`, so a failed sign-in or a choice of organizations is shown there; its organization field is then prefilled with the remembered organization. The organization page's **Not your organization?** link forgets the remembered organization before it returns to `/login`, so the landing page stays put; it is also the way out when the remembered organization no longer exists and the page says there is no organization by that name.

No route asks about an email first: the page offers every method up front, and the password login answers a generic `401`, so nothing tells whether an email has a user anywhere. What the page does disclose, to anyone who knows an organization's id, is that the organization exists and the names and provider kinds of the configurations its login offers, as any SSO login page does; the id is already public as the organization's hostname, and the configurations are the buttons the page shows. A signed-in member of several organizations switches between them without signing in again: the account menu's **Organizations** list posts `POST /api/auth/org/switch { organizationId }`, which re-establishes the session for the chosen membership and reloads the portal.

### Password

The form posts email + password to the organization's login route, which verifies the credential and **establishes a browser session** — there is no client-held token. The `fetch` uses `credentials: 'include'` so the gateway's `Set-Cookie` is stored even cross-origin:

```text
1. POST /api/auth/org/login/<organizationId> { email, password }   (credentials: 'include')
2. OrganizationLoginHandler.handleLogin → AuthEndpointSupport.handlePasswordLogin:
   - LocalAuthenticationService.authenticateOrganizationUser(email, password)
       finds the organization user with that email (a system user or an application
       user with the same email is another row and never signs in here), requires it
       enabled, loads its IdentityCredential and verifies the bcrypt hash; an
       organization user with no password fails here
   - ParticipantIdentityService.resolveParticipant(user.id, organizationId, null)
       requires the organization user's enabled OrganizationMembership of that
       organization and makes the OrganizationParticipant from the two
   - on success: establishSession(ctx, participant) puts it on the Vert.x session
                 (regenerating the session id), then 204 + Set-Cookie
   - on any failure: 401 "Invalid credentials"
                     (deliberately generic — covers unknown email, wrong password,
                      no password, disabled user or membership, not a member)
3. OrganizationLoginPage.vue calls userState.login() → Kinotic.connect().
   The default resolution supplies no auth headers in a browser, so the
   WebSocket upgrade is authenticated by the session cookie set in step 2.
```

The SPA never exchanges the password for a token and never sends raw passwords over the WebSocket. Non-UI clients (CLI, automation) do not use this path — they authenticate directly at the upgrade instead; the table in "The WebSocket upgrade" below covers what each client type presents.

### A provider the organization offers

Each button on the organization's page is a form posting to the organization's start route for that configuration. The route also answers `GET`, so a link — from a bookmark, or from the organization's own tile in its provider's application launcher — starts the same flow:

```text
1. POST|GET /api/auth/org/login/<organizationId>/start/<configId>?referer=<spa-path>
   - the router guard bounced an unauthenticated navigation to /login?referer=<spa-path>,
     and the login pages forward it here; a provider sign-in leaves the SPA, so the path
     cannot be kept client side the way the password path keeps it
2. OrganizationLoginHandler.handleStart:
   - an enabled OrgSignupOidcConfiguration under that id, which every organization's
     login offers; otherwise the organization's own configuration under it
     (oidcConfigurationService.findOffered(configId, organizationId, null)); 400 for
     anything else
   - stashes the organization on the flow session, with the referer when it names a
     path within the SPA, then state/nonce/PKCE as for signup, and 302 to the IdP
   - the completed login is bound to the page that started it, or to the portal when a
     GET link, which names no page, started it; a page that is neither the portal nor one
     kinotic.domain.cors.allowedOriginPattern names is not recorded, and the flow returns to
     the portal holding no login for it
3. IdP returns to the callback registered for the configuration:
     GET /api/auth/org/login/social/callback/<configId>   an org sign-up registration
     GET /api/auth/org/login/sso/callback/<configId>      the organization's own configuration
4. OrganizationLoginHandler → AuthEndpointSupport.completeOidcLogin:
   - validates state/nonce, exchanges code, validates id_token (sub + email_verified)
   - looks up the organization user bound to (configId, sub) (ParticipantIdentityService.
     findOrganizationUserByOidcIdentity) and its OrganizationMembership of the stashed
     organization
   - no organization user bound to the identity: through the organization's own
                 configuration, the member an administrator added under the identity's
                 verified email that nobody has signed in as yet is claimed — the identity
                 is bound to that organization user as its first sign-in method and it
                 signs in; otherwise 302 /login?error=no_user
   - no membership: 302 /login?error=no_user
   - a disabled organization user or membership: 302 /login?error=user_disabled
   - otherwise: establishSession(ctx, participant), then redirectSuccess → 302 to the
       stored referer, or the SPA root when the flow stored none, with Set-Cookie.
       No token travels in the URL.
5. The SPA loads with the session cookie set; userState.login() opens the realtime
   connection, authenticated by that cookie.
```

### Social button on the landing page

The landing page's buttons are populated from `GET /api/auth/org/login/providers`, which lists the unique provider keys present in the org sign-up configs (the invite-hint UI on `MembersPage` reads the same endpoint). A sign-in there names no organization, so its callback finds the one organization the identity is a member of:

```text
1. POST /api/auth/org/login/social/start/github?referer=<spa-path>
2. OrganizationLoginHandler.handleSocialStart:
   - finds the OrgSignupOidcConfiguration with provider="github"
     (oidcConfigurationService.findEnabledOrgSignupByProvider)
   - same flow-session setup as above, with no organization stashed, then 302 to the IdP
3. IdP returns to GET /api/auth/org/login/social/callback/<configId>
4. OrganizationLoginHandler.handleSocialCallback → completeOidcLogin:
   - finds the organization user bound to (configId, sub) and its enabled memberships
     (OrganizationMembershipService.findMemberships)
   - exactly one: signs in to that organization as above
   - no organization user, or no membership: 302 /login?error=no_user
   - a disabled organization user, or one whose every membership is disabled:
     302 /login?error=user_disabled
   - several: their ids are kept in the session for the page that started the flow and
     302 /login?error=multiple_organizations&referer=<spa-path> — the user has proven who
     it is, so the landing page reads the ids from GET /api/auth/org/login/choices, answered
     for two minutes and until the page starts a login at an organization, and offers those
     organizations to choose from; the person signs in at the chosen one's own page, which
     lands on the referer. The redirect carries no ids, so the page that started the flow
     learns only the code
```

### Finding one's organizations

`POST /api/auth/org/login/find { email, turnstileToken }` emails the address every organization its organization user holds an enabled membership of, each with a link to that organization's login page (`OrganizationService.sendMembershipsEmail`); a disabled organization user is told of none, as it can sign in to none. The route always answers `204` and the email is sent whether or not the address belongs to any organization — one that belongs to none says so — so the request reveals nothing about the address. With `KINOTIC_EMAIL_ENABLED=false` the links are logged to the management server's console instead of sent.

The route is open to anyone and sends an email on every call, so it requires a person at the browser: a Cloudflare Turnstile token earned on the page, verified by the management server with the site's secret (`TurnstileVerifier`, configured under `kinotic.managementServer.turnstile.*`). `GET /api/auth/org/login/find` answers `{turnstileSiteKey}`, the site whose challenge the landing page renders before it enables the button, and a request whose token is missing, already verified or refused answers `400`. An environment with no Turnstile site, such as the e2e stack, turns the requirement off with `kinotic.managementServer.turnstile.enabled=false`, and the `GET` answers `{}`; development uses Cloudflare's always-passing test site.

### System users (SYSTEM scope)

A system user is a `SystemParticipantIdentity` (type `SYSTEM_USER`): unique by email among system users, acting in the system scope alone. The same email may also be an organization user and a user of any application, each with its own password. System users sign in through a separate, password-only route used by the system console (there is no signup, SSO, or social path for SYSTEM scope):

```text
1. POST /api/auth/system/login { email, password }   (credentials: 'include')
2. SystemLoginHandler.handleLogin → AuthEndpointSupport.handlePasswordLogin:
   - LocalAuthenticationService.authenticateSystemUser(email, password)
       verifies the system user's password, then resolveParticipant(user.id, null, null)
       makes its SystemParticipant — an organization user or an application user, even
       with the same email, is another row and can never authenticate here
   - success/failure behave exactly like the org password branch:
     204 + Set-Cookie, or a generic 401
```

The session established here is the same browser-session mechanism as every other login path; `/api/auth/me` and `/api/auth/logout` apply unchanged.

The console lists them at **Members → Users**, read-only, from `SystemMemberService.findUsers` in the system zone, which lists the `SystemParticipantIdentity` rows. System users are created outside the console — by the migration fixtures, or by the identity provider once SYSTEM scope is behind Entra — so the page reports who holds access rather than granting it.

### The WebSocket upgrade (the final step in every path)

Authentication happens at the WebSocket upgrade (handshake), not in a STOMP CONNECT frame. How the upgrade is authenticated depends on the client:

<table>
<thead>
  <tr>
    <th>
      Client
    </th>
    
    <th>
      Upgrade credentials
    </th>
  </tr>
</thead>

<tbody>
  <tr>
    <td>
      Browser SPA
    </td>
    
    <td>
      Session cookie established by the REST login; the default credential resolution supplies no headers
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      Node client, credentials
    </td>
    
    <td>
      <code>
        clientId
      </code>
      
      , <code>
        clientSecret
      </code>
      
      , plus <code>
        organizationId
      </code>
      
       / <code>
        applicationId
      </code>
      
       scope headers (via <code>
        BasicCredentialsResolver
      </code>
      
       or the <code>
        KINOTIC_CLIENT_*
      </code>
      
       environment variables)
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      Node client, Bearer token
    </td>
    
    <td>
      <code>
        Authorization: Bearer <jwt>
      </code>
      
       (via <code>
        BearerCredentialsResolver
      </code>

      </code>
      
       / <code>
        applicationId
      </code>
      
       claims
    </td>
  </tr>
</tbody>
</table>

The browser SPA never holds a JWT — its login establishes a session cookie and that cookie authenticates the upgrade. The Bearer path is for non-browser clients: the CLI obtains an access token through the OAuth device-code grant at `POST /api/auth/oauth/token`, which mints a Kinotic JWT carrying `sub` / `email` / `organizationId` / `applicationId`. For that path the management server validates the JWT signature against its signing keys and creates the `Session`. Every path admits only the server's own kind of participant: a credential that proves an identity of another scope fails as invalid (see [System Security](https://kinotic.ai/platform/system-security#authentication-methods)). The CLI persists a rotating refresh token to mint fresh access tokens before each connect.

## Provider-Specific Quirks

OIDC is a standard, but providers diverge on a few details. The validation helpers in `OAuth2Util` (`isIssuerValid`, `isEmailVerified`) handle these declaratively — the provider key on `OidcConfiguration` selects the right behaviour. No provider needs handler-level branching: a row either has an `authority` for OIDC discovery — derived from the organization's `providerAccount` for an organization's row, seeded for a curated one — or, for a curated row only, sets `authorizationUri`/`tokenUri`/`userInfoUri`/`userEmailsUri`/`scopes` explicitly, and every handler consumes the same claims shape either way.

`isEmailVerified` and `isIssuerValid` are the only places these differences live in code. Adding a curated provider doesn't require code changes — an OIDC-compliant provider seeds a row with an `authority`, and a plain-OAuth2 provider seeds a row with explicit endpoint fields; only providers with non-standard claim quirks (Apple's first-login-only email, Microsoft's `/common` issuer template) need to be classified explicitly in those helpers. Offering a type to organizations is one line on `OidcProviderType`: its issuer template and the pattern the organization's account must match.

## Per-Org SSO Configuration

An `OrganizationOidcConfiguration` is offered at the org's own login page, `/login/<organizationId>`, by existing. An organization admin manages the organization's configurations in the portal under **Organization settings → Authentication providers**, or through the published `OwnedOidcConfigurationService` the page calls (`Kinotic.ownedOidcConfigurations` in `@kinotic-ai/management-api`, and an MCP tool), which acts for the caller's organization alone.

1. **Add provider** opens the form in a drawer on the right. Pick the provider (Google, Microsoft or Okta) and enter the display name the login page prints on its button, the organization's account at the provider where the kind takes one (the **Directory (tenant) ID** for Microsoft Entra ID, the **Okta domain** on `okta.com`, `oktapreview.com` or `okta-emea.com` for Okta), the client ID and the client secret, or tick **Public client (no secret)**. The form checks the account against the kind's pattern before it saves, and shows the server's message when the server still refuses. The audience is optional, under **Advanced**. Saving calls `OwnedOidcConfigurationService.save(configuration, clientSecret)`: the authority is derived from the kind's template, so no URL is given, and the `organizationId` is the caller's whatever was sent. A secret is held in the organization's own scope of the secret storage — the row itself never names one, and nothing reads it back through the service; `confidentialClient` says whether one is held. `createUserOnSignIn` is refused on an organization's configuration, and the form does not offer it: the organization's administrators add its members (see [Members](#members)), and the provider signs in the member it verifies under a pending member's address, claiming that organization user on the first sign-in, or the organization user its identity is already bound to. A person the provider verifies whose address is no member's gets `no_user`; one whose address already has an organization user that someone signs in as is not claimed, and joins by accepting the invitation the administrator's Add member sent.
2. Once saved, the form shows the configuration's **callback URL**, `<kinotic.managementApi.apiBaseUrl>/api/auth/org/login/sso/callback/<configId>`, which `OwnedOidcConfigurationService.findCallbackUrl(configId)` returns. Add it to the IdP app registration as a redirect URI; sign-ins through the configuration fail until it is there. It is the only one the configuration needs: a login, an invitation accepted through the provider, and a member connecting the provider to their organization user from the Profile page all return to it, and the flow's purpose, recorded on the session when it starts, says which it is. For a same-origin deploy that base is the portal's own origin; for a split-origin deploy (the SPA on the sites Worker, the backend on AKS) it is the backend's hostname, so the IdP returns the browser to the management server, not the SPA. The provider's row, its **Edit** form and its details all show the same URL again.
3. Editing a configuration leaves its kind fixed, since the kind is the scope it is offered at and the server refuses a save that changes it. The client secret field starts empty: a save with it empty keeps the secret held (`save` with a null or blank secret keeps it), and a secret entered replaces it. **Make this a public client**, which asks for confirmation, deletes the held secret with `OwnedOidcConfigurationService.deleteClientSecret(configId)`.
4. The row menu also enables or disables the configuration (a disabled one is listed on no login page and signs no one in), deletes it after a confirmation (sign-ins through it stop at once and its held secret is deleted), and copies it to an application: **Copy to application** calls `OwnedOidcConfigurationService.copy(configurationId, applicationId)`, which makes an `ApplicationOidcConfiguration` with the source's provider, account, client ID and secret, and shows the copy's own callback URL, `<the application's API host>/api/auth/app/login/oidc/callback/<copyId>`, to register with the provider as well. The application's API host is its label under `kinotic.domain.appApiBaseUrl`.

A user who logs in via this path lands at the `/api/auth/org/login/sso/callback/:configId` handler — the IdP doesn't care that the configId is org-scoped instead of system-scoped. The provider's application launcher can link straight to `<kinotic.managementApi.apiBaseUrl>/api/auth/org/login/<organizationId>/start/<configId>`, which starts the same flow from a plain `GET`; the form and the row's details show it as the **Direct sign-in link**.

## System Authentication

System users (`SystemParticipantIdentity`) sign in to the system server with an email and password, `POST /api/auth/system/login`, and the plan is to move it to Microsoft Entra, separate from the routes documented above. The system login authenticates system users alone, so an organization user is refused there as a wrong password is, and every organization login authenticates organization users alone, so a system user is refused there the same way. A person who is both signs in to each with that scope's own user and password. The curated social providers are intentionally limited to end-user self-service signup and grant org-scoped access only, so no organization route can produce a `SYSTEM`-scoped session.

The app server serves every application at an API host of its own, `<organizationId>--<applicationId>` under `kinotic.domain.appApiBaseUrl` (see [Configuration](https://kinotic.ai/platform/configuration#application-api-hosts)). Its login and OAuth routes act for the application whose host the request is addressed to and answer `404` on any other host, and that host is the application's OAuth issuer. The one exception is a sign-in through a system social registration (`ApplicationSocialOidcConfiguration`): a provider returns the browser only to a redirect URI registered in advance, and the registration is shared by every application that offers it, so its `authorize` and `callback` routes are served at `kinotic.domain.appApiBaseUrl` itself, the shared host, and the verified sign-in is handed to the application's own host under a single-use code (`SocialLoginHandoffService`, an Ignite cache with a one-minute TTL) where the session is established. The code completes the sign-in only in the browser that started it: the start at the application's host put a value in that browser's session, the shared host carries it through its own session into the handoff, and the completion requires the browser to present it again, so a completion URL passed to another person signs no one in.

CORS for the server's UI origin is applied at the router root. A Vert.x `SessionHandler` covers every `/api/*` route (and the STOMP WebSocket path), so the same session cookie carries the OIDC roundtrip state and the post-login identity; the cookie is `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Lax`, with a configurable timeout (`kinotic.api-gateway.session-timeout`).

Routes are namespaced under `/api/auth/...`. Organization login and signup are the SPA's paths; the application-login, OAuth, and invite routes are listed for completeness.

      Owner
    </th>
    
    <th>

    </th>
  </tr>
</thead>

# CRI Format

> Kinotic Resource Identifier specification.

## Overview

A CRI (Kinotic Resource Identifier) is used by Kinotic to route requests to the appropriate service, method, or event stream. It is a URI-like format with parts named for clarity within the Kinotic platform.

## Format

```text
scheme://[scope@][zone~]resourceName[/path][#version]
```

Everything in brackets (`[]`) is optional.

## Case

Every part keeps the case it was written with, and addresses match by exact string comparison — `OrderService` and `OrderService` are two different addresses. Service names carry the case of the class that published them, so a typical address looks like:

```text
srv://management-api~org.kinotic.management.api.services.ProjectService/findByRepoFullName
```

## Components

### Scheme

Identifies the type of resource being addressed.

<table>
<thead>
  <tr>
    <th>
      Scheme
    </th>
    
    <th>
      Description
    </th>
  </tr>
</thead>

<tbody>
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        srv
      </code>
    </td>
    
    <td>
      Published services and their methods
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        stream
      </code>
    </td>
    
    <td>
      Event streams (not yet routable through the gateway)
    </td>
  </tr>
</tbody>
</table>

### Scope

An optional qualifier that narrows the CRI to a specific context, such as a tenant ID, user ID, or device ID. When present, it appears before the `@` symbol.

If a scope needs sub-scopes, use the format `scope:sub-scope`.

```text
srv://tenant-123@app.acme-org.orders-app~OrderService
stream://device-42@app.acme-org.orders-app~temperature/sensor-1
```

### Zone

The optional zone places the resource in the isolation boundary the gateway validates on every send and subscribe. It precedes the resourceName, separated by `~`. A zone is one or more dot-separated labels of lowercase letters, digits, and interior dashes.

<table>
<thead>
  <tr>
    <th>
      Zone
    </th>
    
    <th>
      Description
    </th>
  </tr>
</thead>

<tbody>
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        app.<organizationId>.<applicationId>
      </code>
    </td>
    
    <td>
      One application's services. Only that application's participants and the owning organization's runtimes can call them, through the app server, the one server that reaches these zones; they are hosted by the owning organization's runtime, which authenticates as an organization participant. Applications may nest their own sub-zones, e.g. <code>
        app.acme-org.orders-app.billing
      </code>
      
      .
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        app-api
      </code>
    </td>
    
    <td>
      The platform's data plane for applications, such as entity persistence and named query execution. Hosted in-process by the platform only.
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        management-api
      </code>
    </td>
    
    <td>
      The platform services organizations manage the system through, such as member, application, and entity definition management. Hosted in-process by the platform only.
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        system-api
      </code>
    </td>
    
    <td>
      The system's own services. Only system participants can call or host them.
    </td>
  </tr>
</tbody>
</table>

A cluster member outside the platform's servers can host its services in `management-api`, where organizations' users call them through the management server as they call the platform's own; such a service checks the caller's organization itself.

Organization and application ids become zone labels, but only ever after the `app` prefix, so they cannot collide with the platform's own zones. The one exception is guarded explicitly: creating an organization or application whose name slugifies to `system-api` is rejected.

Which zones a connection may address is determined by the authenticated participant. A participant may also address any sub-zone of a zone it is allowed, so `app.acme-org.orders-app.billing` is reachable by whoever may reach `app.acme-org.orders-app`. An address without a `~` carries no zone at all and is only reachable by system participants.

Each server also has a zone partitioning, the zones it hosts and the zones it reaches. A node advertises a service
to the cluster only in a zone its server hosts, and sends only to zones its server reaches: an address in any
other zone has no handlers there. An address without a zone passes both.

The gateway applies the partitioning before a frame reaches the event bus: a send to a zone the server does not
reach, or a subscription in a zone it does not host, is refused whatever the participant may address. The
service directory and listener monitors still see every registration in the cluster, so a service hosted by one
server shows as online from any other, while each server's MCP listing shows only the tools in zones it reaches.

### Resource Name

The name of the resource being addressed, excluding the zone. For services, this is the fully qualified service name. For streams, this is the event type name.

```text
srv://management-api~com.example.UserService
stream://app.acme-org.orders-app~temperature
```

### Path

An optional path that identifies a specific part of the resource, such as a method name on a service. The path's case is preserved.

```text
srv://management-api~com.example.UserService/findById
stream://app.acme-org.orders-app~temperature/sensor-1
```

### Version

An optional semantic version for the resource. Enables versioned service routing so multiple versions of a service can coexist.

```text
srv://management-api~com.example.UserService/findById#1.0.0
srv://management-api~com.example.UserService#2.0.0
```

## Factory Function

The `createCRI` function provides several overloads for constructing CRI instances:

```typescript
import { createCRI } from '@kinotic-ai/core'

// From a raw string
const cri1 = createCRI('srv://management-api~com.example.UserService/findById#1.0.0')

// From scheme and resource name (which may carry a zone)
const cri2 = createCRI('srv', 'management-api~com.example.UserService')

// From scheme, scope, and resource name
const cri3 = createCRI('stream', 'tenant-123', 'app.acme-org.orders-app~orders')

// From all components
const cri4 = createCRI('srv', null, 'management-api~com.example.UserService', 'findById', '1.0.0')
```

### CRI Interface

The `CRI` interface provides methods to access each component:

```typescript
const cri = createCRI('srv://tenant-123@app.acme-org.orders-app~OrderService/placeOrder#2.0.0')

cri.scheme()        // 'srv'
cri.scope()         // 'tenant-123'
cri.hasScope()      // true
cri.zone()          // 'app.acme-org.orders-app'
cri.hasZone()       // true
cri.resourceName()  // 'OrderService'
cri.path()          // 'placeOrder'
cri.hasPath()       // true
cri.version()       // '2.0.0'
cri.hasVersion()    // true
cri.baseResource()  // 'srv://tenant-123@app.acme-org.orders-app~OrderService'
cri.raw()           // 'srv://tenant-123@app.acme-org.orders-app~OrderService/placeOrder#2.0.0'
```
